Fixed-point decimal vectors

Source: R/decimal.R
decimal128.Rd

decimal128() creates a vector of DuckDB's DECIMAL(precision, scale): numbers with at most precision digits, scale of them after the point, held exactly as a 128-bit integer coefficient. A DuckDB DECIMAL column, or one written to it, keeps every digit and its type.

Usage

decimal128(x = character(), precision = 38L, scale = 0L)

is_decimal128(x)

decimal_precision(x)

decimal_scale(x)

Arguments

x

For decimal128(), a vector to convert; for is_decimal128(), any object; for decimal_precision() and decimal_scale(), a decimal128 vector.

precision

The number of digits, 1 to 38.

scale

The number of digits after the point, 0 to precision.

Value

decimal128() returns a decimal128 vector the length of x. is_decimal128() returns TRUE or FALSE, and decimal_precision() and decimal_scale() a single integer.

Details

x can be text, a logical, integer or double vector, a zuint vector, a bit64 integer64 or another decimal128.

  • Text is read as DuckDB reads a DECIMAL: an optional sign, digits with an optional point, _ between digits, an exponent, and surrounding whitespace; digits past the scale round half away from zero. "NA" and blank strings are NA.

  • Integers and zuint vectors convert exactly.

  • A double is rounded to the scale, half away from zero, as DuckDB's cast does: decimal128(2.675, 5, 2) is 2.68.

  • A decimal128 of another type is rescaled, rounding half away from zero. Without precision or scale it keeps its own: decimal128(x, 20) changes only the precision. With neither it is returned as it is.

A value that does not fit precision digits becomes NA with a warning of class zuint_cast_warning. Names are kept.

Arithmetic follows DuckDB's types: + and - keep the larger scale and grow the precision by one, * adds precisions and scales, and precision stops at 38. As in DuckDB, a product of two operands of at most 18 digits stops at 18 unless its scale is 18 or more. A result that does not fit is NA with a zuint_overflow_warning. An integer operand counts as DECIMAL(10, 0), int64 as DECIMAL(19, 0), uint64 as DECIMAL(20, 0) and the 128-bit types as DECIMAL(38, 0). A whole double is an integer operand, typed as DuckDB types an integer literal; any other double follows options(zuint.double).

Comparison is exact across scales, and with every integer and whole double, even one too large for 38 digits. /, %%, %/% and ^ compute in double, as do mean(), median(), prod() and the Math functions other than those below; !, & and | give logicals.

These keep a decimal type, DuckDB's:

  • abs(), cummax() and cummin() keep the type, and sum() and cumsum() are DECIMAL(38, scale).

  • round(x, digits) rounds half away from zero to DECIMAL(precision, digits), and is x when digits is the scale or more. A negative digits gives scale 0, with one more digit at scale 0.

  • floor(), ceiling() and trunc() are DECIMAL(precision, 0).

c(), vctrs and x[i] <- value combine values in DuckDB's common type (for [<-, x's type): the largest scale and the most integer digits, and the scale cut when both do not fit 38 digits. A value the type cannot hold exactly is NA with a zuint_cast_warning; only decimal128() rounds. sum(), min() and the other Summary functions dispatch on their first argument, as R's group generics do, so write sum(x, 1L), not sum(1L, x).

Examples

price <- decimal128(c("19.99", "5.00", NA), 10, 2)
price
#> <decimal128(10, 2)[3]>
#> [1] 19.99  5.00    NA
price * 3L
#> <decimal128(18, 2)[3]>
#> [1] 59.97 15.00    NA
sum(price, na.rm = TRUE)
#> <decimal128(38, 2)[1]>
#> [1] 24.99
decimal_scale(price * price)
#> [1] 4

# Too many digits, so NA with a warning:
decimal128("123.45", 4, 2)
#> Warning: 1 value could not be represented as decimal128(4, 2) and became NA.
#> <decimal128(4, 2)[1]>
#> [1] NA
